Treatment: topical antibiotic; supportive care, hygiene, lubricants (no antibiotic); antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops, avoid allergen.

questions.question: Write counselling points on the correct use of eye drops.
questions.answer: Wash hands; check label and expiry; tilt the head back and pull down the lower lid to form a pocket; instil one drop without the dropper touching the eye or lashes; close the eye gently for 1–2 minutes and press the inner corner (nasolacrimal occlusion) to keep the drug in the eye and reduce systemic absorption; wipe excess; wait 5 minutes between different drops; apply ointment last; remove contact lenses unless advised; discard opened drops after 4 weeks; never share.

questions.question: Write about antimicrobial stewardship.
questions.answer:
Definition: coordinated programme to promote appropriate use of antimicrobials (right drug, dose, route, duration) to improve outcomes and limit resistance.
Components: hospital antibiotic policy and guidelines; restricted reserve antibiotics needing approval; culture before antibiotics; de-escalation to narrow-spectrum drug after culture; IV-to-oral switch; shortest effective duration; dose optimisation; audit and feedback; infection-control team; education of staff; surveillance of resistance and consumption.
Team: physician, microbiologist, clinical pharmacist, infection-control nurse.

questions.question: Name the drugs used in open-angle glaucoma with their adverse effects.
questions.answer:
Prostaglandin analogues – latanoprost, bimatoprost: conjunctival redness, darkening of iris, longer lashes.
Beta-blockers – timolol: bronchospasm, bradycardia, heart block (avoid in asthma, COPD).
Alpha-2 agonists – brimonidine: allergy, dry mouth, fatigue; avoid in infants.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors – dorzolamide: stinging, bitter taste; acetazolamide oral: paraesthesia, diuresis, hypokalaemia, renal stones.
Miotics – pilocarpine: small pupil, dim vision, brow ache.
Rho-kinase inhibitor – netarsudil: red eye.

questions.question: What is the Red Line campaign?
questions.answer: An Indian awareness campaign (2016) in which packs of prescription-only antibiotics carry a vertical red line, telling people not to use them without a doctor's prescription.

questions.question: What is the normal intraocular pressure?
questions.answer: About 10–21 mmHg.

questions.question: Define polycystic ovary syndrome. Write its diagnostic criteria, pathogenesis, clinical features and management.
questions.answer:
1. Definition: common endocrine–metabolic disorder of reproductive-age women with anovulation, androgen excess and polycystic ovaries, often with insulin resistance.
2. Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3): oligo/anovulation; clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism; polycystic ovaries on ultrasound – after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, CAH, Cushing's, tumours.
3. Pathogenesis: insulin resistance → hyperinsulinaemia → ovarian androgens ↑, SHBG ↓; raised LH:FSH; follicles arrest → anovulation.
4. Features: irregular/absent periods, infertility, hirsutism, acne, scalp hair thinning, obesity, acanthosis nigricans; long-term – diabetes, dyslipidaemia, CVD, endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, depression.
5. Non-drug: weight loss 5–10%, diet, exercise, cosmetic hair removal, screening.
6. Drugs: COCs (cycle control, reduce androgens); cyclic progestin for endometrial protection; anti-androgens – spironolactone, cyproterone, finasteride with contraception; eflornithine cream; metformin for insulin resistance; ovulation induction – letrozole or clomiphene; gonadotropins/IVF by specialists.
7. Counselling: lifestyle is key, hirsutism improves over 6 months, metformin with meals, regular check-ups.

questions.question: Define dysmenorrhoea. Differentiate primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea and write the management of primary dysmenorrhoea.
questions.answer:
1. Definition: painful menstruation with crampy lower abdominal pain before or during periods, affecting daily activity.
2. Primary: no pelvic disease; begins 6–12 months after menarche; pain starts with bleeding, lasts 1–3 days; normal examination; due to prostaglandins.
3. Secondary: due to endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, IUD; later onset; pain may start before and continue after period; dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding.
4. Pathogenesis (primary): progesterone withdrawal → endometrial PGF2α, PGE2 → strong uterine contractions and ischaemia → pain, nausea, diarrhoea, headache.
5. Features: lower abdominal cramps radiating to back and thighs, nausea, vomiting, loose stools, fatigue.
6. Non-drug: local heat, exercise, yoga, rest, stop smoking, TENS.
7. Drugs: NSAIDs first-line – mefenamic acid, ibuprofen, naproxen started at onset of pain/bleeding and taken regularly 2–3 days; paracetamol; antispasmodics (drotaverine, dicyclomine); combined oral contraceptives or progestin methods.
8. Refer if not relieved, late onset, heavy bleeding, fever, dyspareunia.
9. Counselling: take NSAID early with food.

questions.question: Define premenstrual syndrome. Write its clinical features, diagnosis and management.
questions.answer:
1. Definition: recurrent physical, emotional and behavioural symptoms in the luteal phase that resolve within a few days of menstruation, affecting daily life; severe form PMDD.
2. Etiopathogenesis: abnormal sensitivity to normal cyclical oestrogen and progesterone changes, altered serotonin and GABA activity; stress, family history, lifestyle.
3. Features: irritability, mood swings, depression, anxiety, poor concentration, food cravings; breast tenderness, bloating, weight gain, headache, fatigue, acne.
4. Diagnosis: prospective symptom diary for at least 2 cycles, symptoms limited to luteal phase; exclude depression, anxiety, thyroid disease.
5. Non-drug: education, diary, aerobic exercise, sleep, stress reduction, CBT, less salt, caffeine, sugar and alcohol; calcium supplement.
6. Drugs: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) continuous or luteal-phase for PMDD/severe mood symptoms; COCs with drospirenone; NSAIDs for pain; spironolactone for bloating and breast tenderness; GnRH analogues with add-back for refractory cases.
7. Counselling: plan ahead using diary, lifestyle, take medicines as directed, seek help for severe mood symptoms.

questions.question: Write the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS.
questions.answer:
Diagnosis requires any two of three, after excluding other causes (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, androgen-secreting tumour):
1. Oligo-ovulation or anovulation (infrequent or absent periods).
2. Clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, alopecia) or biochemical hyperandrogenism (raised testosterone).
3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (many small follicles and/or increased ovarian volume).

questions.question: Write the role of NSAIDs in dysmenorrhoea with counselling points.
questions.answer:
Primary dysmenorrhoea is caused by excess endometrial prostaglandins; NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen, naproxen) inhibit COX and reduce prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing uterine contractions and pain; they also reduce menstrual blood loss.
Counselling: start at the first sign of pain or bleeding (or a day before if periods are predictable) and take regularly for 2–3 days rather than waiting for severe pain; take with food; avoid if peptic ulcer, kidney disease or aspirin-sensitive asthma; use heat and exercise as well; see a doctor if pain is not relieved.

questions.question: Write the drug management of PCOS based on the patient's needs.
questions.answer:
Irregular cycles / endometrial protection: combined oral contraceptives or cyclic progestin.
Hirsutism and acne: COCs first; anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone, finasteride) only with contraception; topical eflornithine; acne treatment.
Insulin resistance, weight: metformin; lifestyle; weight-loss drugs in selected.
Infertility: letrozole (often first) or clomiphene for ovulation induction; metformin add-on; gonadotropins, ovarian drilling, IVF.
All: lifestyle change, screening for diabetes and lipids.

questions.question: Write the non-pharmacological management of premenstrual syndrome.
questions.answer: Keep a symptom diary to recognise the pattern and plan; education and reassurance; regular aerobic exercise; adequate sleep; stress management (yoga, relaxation, CBT); small frequent meals with complex carbohydrates; reduce salt (bloating), caffeine, sugar and alcohol in the luteal phase; stop smoking; calcium-rich diet or supplements; support from family.

questions.question: What is acanthosis nigricans and its significance in PCOS?
questions.answer: Dark, thickened, velvety skin in body folds (neck, armpits); it is a sign of insulin resistance, common in women with PCOS.

questions.question: Which oral contraceptive progestin is preferred in premenstrual syndrome?
questions.answer: Drospirenone (combined with ethinylestradiol), which has anti-mineralocorticoid and anti-androgenic activity and helps PMS/PMDD symptoms.
